forces.title: West Asia crisis inflates raw material and natural gas import costs
forces.description: The ongoing West Asia geopolitical crisis has led to sharp increases in international prices of urea, DAP, and key raw materials like ammonia (up ~60%), sulphur (up ~50%), phosphoric acid, and natural gas (up ~$5/mmbtu to ~$15/mmbtu). This heightens cost pressures across the sector, as India is highly import-dependent on Gulf countries for over 80% of ammonia and sulphur and 63% of natural gas, making supplies vulnerable to Strait of Hormuz disruptions.

forces.title: FY27 fertiliser subsidy budget likely insufficient due to elevated import prices
forces.description: The budgeted fertiliser subsidy of Rs 1.71 lakh crore for FY27 (Rs 1.17 lakh crore for urea, Rs 0.54 lakh crore for NBS) is expected to fall short. The recent surge in import prices of natural gas, raw materials, and finished fertilisers, driven by the West Asia crisis, will necessitate significant supplementary grants. This places a strain on government finances and indicates potential under-recoveries or payment delays for the industry, especially given fixed retail prices.

forces.title: Below-normal monsoon forecast poses risk to fertiliser demand
forces.description: The Indian Meteorological Department's (IMD) forecast of a below-normal monsoon for CY2026 at 92% of the long period average (LPA) introduces a key variable for fertiliser demand in FY27. Uneven rainfall distribution could lead to regional demand variability, potentially impacting overall consumption despite current healthy reservoir levels and increasing minimum support prices (MSPs) for major crops. Monsoon progression remains a crucial monitorable.

forces.title: Increasing fertiliser import dependency amplifies geopolitical vulnerability
forces.description: India's overall fertiliser import dependency increased significantly to ~34% in FY26 from ~23% in FY25, particularly for Urea (~29-30%) and DAP (~68%). This rising reliance on international markets, especially West Asia (37% of urea imports from region in 10MFY26, 40% of DAP imports from Saudi Arabia), makes the sector highly vulnerable to global supply disruptions and price volatility stemming from geopolitical events like the West Asia crisis and Strait of Hormuz blockage.

forces.title: Fixed MRP and high import costs create significant under-recovery for DAP
forces.description: International DAP prices surged to around USD 900/MT (Rs 83,500/MT) in April 2026, nearly doubling pre-West Asia conflict levels. Despite the government fixing the Maximum Retail Price (MRP) at Rs 27,000/MT and providing a subsidy of Rs 30,000/MT (plus a special Rs 3,500/MT package), imports remain economically unviable. This leaves an under-recovery of nearly Rs 23,000/MT, highlighting severe profitability challenges and increasing the need for further government intervention amid elevated prices.

forces.title: Global urea prices soar by 85% MoM due to supply disruptions
forces.description: In April 2026, international urea prices witnessed a sharp month-on-month increase of approximately 85%, reaching $950/tonne. This significant price hike is primarily attributed to major disruptions in fertiliser and natural gas supplies caused by the West Asia conflict and the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz. Such volatility intensifies cost pressures for urea manufacturers and directly impacts the government's subsidy burden, given India's import reliance.

forces.title: Timely subsidy releases strengthen sector's financial resilience
forces.description: In recent years, the fertiliser sector has benefited from timely subsidy releases, which have reduced receivable build-up and supported working capital management for companies. This improved financial health positions the sector better to absorb current volatility in input prices. Comfortable reservoir levels and a strong inventory position further provide a near-term cushion, mitigating immediate risks for the upcoming Kharif sowing season despite external headwinds.

forces.title: Potential increased borrowings due to elevated prices and subsidy delays
forces.description: The persistence of elevated import prices for fertilisers and raw materials, coupled with potential delays in government subsidy releases, could force fertiliser companies to increase their borrowings. This would be necessary to meet working capital requirements, thereby impacting their financial costs and overall profitability. This risk is amplified if geopolitical disruptions continue to keep international prices high and government fiscal space remains constrained.

forces.title: Government's substantial budget allocation supports chemicals and fertilisers
forces.description: The Union Budget 2025-26 allocated Rs. 1,61,965 crore (US$ 18.7 billion) to the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers. This significant government allocation provides broad policy support and financial backing to the sector. While not solely for fertiliser subsidies, it underscores the government's commitment to the industry, which is crucial for agricultural productivity and food security. Such sustained support helps mitigate some financial pressures arising from market volatility.

viewpoints.title: Fertiliser sector faces challenging FY27 due to West Asia crisis and rising input costs
viewpoints.description: CareEdge Ratings anticipates a challenging operating environment for the fertiliser sector in FY27. The West Asia geopolitical crisis has led to sharp increases in natural gas and other key input prices like ammonia, sulphur, and phosphoric acid. This intensifies cost pressures for companies, particularly NPK players, and is expected to significantly increase the government's fertiliser subsidy requirements. Despite improved credit profiles due to timely subsidy releases in prior years, rising import dependence and a forecast of below-normal monsoon add to the cautious outlook.
